title: Mini case - Valuing a company with P/E and a simple DCF
subtitle: Practical application: combining relative and absolute methods to make a decision
openingQuestion: A company has EPS of 5,000 VND, and the industry average P/E is 12x. Valuing by P/E gives 60,000 VND/share. The same company's DCF model gives 45,000 VND/share. How should you handle this gap?
openingOptions: Treat both results as complementary perspectives: P/E reflects how the market is currently pricing the industry (which may be influenced by sentiment), DCF reflects intrinsic value based on cash flow - a large gap is a signal to investigate the cause, not something to resolve by picking randomly
Always trust P/E completely because it's simpler and faster
Always trust DCF completely because it's more complex, hence more accurate
Just take the simple average of the two numbers with no further analysis
explanation: Professional valuation practice always combines MULTIPLE methods (P/E, EV/EBITDA, DCF...) for a complete picture, called a 'valuation football field'. If the methods produce similar results, confidence rises. If the gap is large (as in this case: 60,000 VND vs 45,000 VND), it's worth investigating why: is the whole industry being priced above its intrinsic value by the market (an inflated P/E), or are the DCF assumptions too conservative (growth and WACC not properly reflecting real prospects)?

diagram.label: Conclude with a reasonable value range

realWorldExample.description: When advising on an IPO or M&A deal, investment banks always present a 'football field' chart - a range of values from different valuation methods (Comps, Precedent Transaction, DCF) stacked on top of each other, helping the client see the full picture instead of a single number.

quiz.question: If a P/E valuation (market-based) is significantly higher than a DCF valuation (intrinsic-based), which of the following is the most reasonable possibility to consider?
options: P/E is always more accurate than DCF, so just take the P/E result as the standard
DCF is always wrong because it's based on forecasts, so it should be discarded entirely
There's no possible explanation for the gap between the two numbers
The whole industry may be being priced by the market above its intrinsic value
quiz.explanation: When a market-based method (P/E, relative) gives a significantly higher result than an intrinsic-based method (DCF, absolute), this is usually a sign of industry-wide overvaluation.

quiz.question: In this valuation case, if you had to give a final investment recommendation based only on two diverging results (P/E: 60,000 VND, DCF: 45,000 VND), which approach shows the most mature financial analysis thinking?
options: Completely ignore the DCF result because P/E is easier for clients to understand
Present both as a value range and clearly explain the assumptions
Always pick the higher number to have an immediate reason to buy
Take the simple average of the two numbers with no further explanation
quiz.explanation: This is the single most important takeaway from both the Stocks track and valuation as a whole: financial valuation is never an exact science - mature thinking shows up in honestly presenting a value range.

quiz.question: A P/E valuation gives 60,000 VND while DCF gives 40,000 VND. What should the next step be?
options: Choose the lower result to be safe when investing
Take the average of the two numbers as the final result
Investigate which assumption is creating that gap
Drop the DCF method because it depends too heavily on assumptions
quiz.explanation: The gap is information, not a nuisance. It says the market is more optimistic than the cash flow you forecast - and the job is to find out who is right, not to average away the question.

quiz.question: Why should an investment recommendation come with a value range instead of a single number?
options: Because different investors have different risk appetites
Because regulations require securities firms to disclose a value range
Because share prices move every session, so one number would go stale
Because every model rests on assumptions that could be wrong
quiz.explanation: A single number creates a false sense of certainty the model never actually had. A value range is more honest, and it shows at what price the investment thesis still holds up.

quiz.question: A valuation gives 55,000 VND, the market price is 54,000 VND. What is the most reasonable conclusion?
options: Almost no margin of safety - not attractive enough to buy
The stock is undervalued, so buy immediately
The model is wrong because the result is too close to the market price
You should buy because any positive gap is a buying opportunity
quiz.explanation: A 2% gap sits comfortably within the margin of error of any model. Value investing requires a cushion thick enough to survive being wrong, not a slightly higher number.

keyTakeaways: Professional valuation practice always combines multiple methods, not just one number
A large gap between methods is a signal for deeper analysis, not something to ignore
The 'valuation football field' - a range from multiple methods - is a standard tool in professional valuation practice

practicePrompt.question: An M&A analyst values a target company using all three methods: DCF gives 8,000 billion, Comps gives 9,500 billion, Precedent Transaction gives 10,200 billion. How should the final result be presented to leadership, and why shouldn't just one number be chosen?
options: Only the highest number (10,200 billion) should be chosen to have the most leverage in negotiations
Multiple methods should be combined and presented as a value range of 8,000-10,200 billion
Only the lowest number (8,000 billion) should be chosen because DCF is always the most accurate method in every case
The simple average of the three numbers should be calculated with no further explanation of the gap
practicePrompt.explanation: Professional valuation practice always combines multiple methods, not just one number. Each method (DCF, Comps, Precedent Transaction) has different strengths/weaknesses - presenting the result as a value range (football field) helps leadership understand the level of uncertainty and the basis for each figure.

application.title: Apply it now
application.message: Pick a stock you're interested in, look up its current P/E, and try roughly calculating a simple DCF valuation (using an estimated FCF and assumed WACC) - see how far apart the two numbers are and why.
application.secondary: If the gap is large, don't jump to a conclusion - investigate which assumption is driving the difference.

sections.text: No professional analyst relies on just one valuation method. This mini case illustrates how to combine P/E (relative valuation) and DCF (absolute valuation) to make a well-grounded investment decision, instead of clinging to a single number.
When two methods give two different results

Suppose a P/E valuation gives 60,000 VND/share, while DCF gives 45,000 VND/share - a significant gap. When a market-based method (P/E, relative) is significantly higher than an intrinsic-based method (DCF, absolute), this is usually a sign that the whole industry is being priced by the market above its true intrinsic value - due to excessive optimism or speculative capital flowing into the sector. This is exactly the kind of warning signal a value investor should stay alert to.

Professional valuation practice always combines MULTIPLE methods (P/E, EV/EBITDA, DCF, Comps, Precedent Transaction...) for a complete picture, called a 'valuation football field'. When advising on an IPO or M&A deal, investment banks always present a football field chart - a range of values from multiple methods stacked on top of each other, helping the client see the full picture instead of a single number. The most mature approach in this case isn't choosing the higher number or taking a simple average, but presenting both results as a reasonable value range (45,000-60,000 VND), clearly explaining the assumptions behind each method, and making a recommendation based on where the current market price sits within that range.

items: Combining multiple methods increases confidence when the results are close together
A large gap between methods is a signal for deeper analysis, not something to ignore
The football field: a standard tool for presenting a value range from multiple methods in professional practice
No valuation method produces an absolutely 'correct' number

lines: Valuation is not an exact science - it is the art of narrowing a zone of uncertainty into a grounded, honest recommendation.
